title: Rational Numbers and Repeating Decimals
summary: What a rational number is, how to show that a decimal is rational, and how to change a repeating decimal into a fraction.

p: A rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. Its decimal form either stops (terminates) or repeats.
Study the table.

Example 6: 0.454545…: two digits repeat, so 100x = 45.4545…; 100x – x = 45, so 99x = 45 and x = 45/99 = 5/11.
Evaluation: 0.444… = 4/9. The difference between 0.333… and 0.333 is that 0.333… = 1/3 exactly while 0.333 = 333/1,000.

title: Irrational Numbers and How to Classify Numbers
summary: What an irrational number is, common examples such as √2 and π, and a decision process for classifying any number, with the answers to the classification exercises.

p: An irrational (non-rational) number cannot be written as a fraction of two integers. Its decimal never ends and never repeats. Examples: most square roots, π and e.

Square roots that are not perfect squares: √2 = 1.41421356…, √3 = 1.7320508…, √5 = 2.2360679…, √7 = 2.6457513… Special numbers: π = 3.14159265…, e = 2.71828182… and the golden ratio φ = 1.6180339… Combinations such as 2 + √3, 5π and √2/2.
Note that √4 = 2 and √9 = 3 are rational, because 4 and 9 are perfect squares.

Step 1: Can it be written as a fraction? If yes, it is rational. Step 2: Is it the square root of a perfect square? Then it is rational. Step 3: Does the decimal stop? Then rational. Step 4: Does the decimal repeat? Then rational. Step 5: If none of these, it is irrational. A decimal such as 0.101001000100001… has a pattern but does not repeat, so it is irrational. So is 0.123456789101112…

Example 10: 5 is rational (5/1). 2/3 is rational. 0.8 is rational (4/5). √25 = 5 is rational. √7 is irrational. π is irrational. 0.666… is rational (2/3). 0.123456789101112… is irrational. –3 is rational. √2 is irrational.
Example 11: 7 rational; √11 irrational; 0.5 rational; π/2 irrational; –4/9 rational; √36 = 6 rational; 2.333… = 7/3 rational; e irrational; 0 rational; √50 irrational.

8 rational; √8 irrational; 0.5 rational; √16 rational; –3/4 rational; π irrational; √100 rational; 0.666… rational; √20 irrational; 2.5 rational; e irrational; √81 rational; 0.123456789… (continuing the pattern) irrational; 7/2 rational; √2 irrational; 0 rational; –5 rational; √(–4) is not a real number at all, so it is neither rational nor irrational; 0.142857142857… rational; √50 irrational.
Why √4 is rational and √5 is not: √4 = 2 = 2/1, but no fraction squared gives exactly 5, and √5 = 2.236067977… never ends or repeats.

title: Properties of Rational and Irrational Numbers and the Real Number System
summary: Closure, density, sums and products of mixed types, the family tree of real numbers, approximating irrationals, and the proof that √2 is irrational.

p: Closure: the sum, difference and product of rational numbers are rational, and so is the quotient (if the divisor is not zero). Example: 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 and 2/3 × 3/4 = 1/2. Density: between any two rational numbers there are infinitely many more. Example: between 1/3 and 1/2, the average is (1/2 + 1/3) ÷ 2 = 5/12, and 1/3 < 5/12 < 1/2.

Irrational numbers are not closed: the sum or product of two irrationals may or may not be irrational. √2 + √2 = 2√2 (irrational), but √2 + (–√2) = 0 (rational). √2 × √3 = √6 (irrational), but √2 × √2 = 2 (rational).
Rational + irrational = irrational: 3 + √2 and 1/2 + π are irrational. Non-zero rational × irrational = irrational: 2√3 and 5π are irrational (but 0 × √2 = 0, the exception).

Real numbers split into rational and irrational numbers. Rational numbers include integers (which include whole numbers, which include natural numbers 1, 2, 3 …) and fractions. Irrational numbers include non-perfect-square roots and special numbers such as π and e.

Example 17: 5 is natural, whole, integer, rational and real. –3 is an integer, rational and real. 2/3 is rational and real. √2 is irrational and real. 0 is whole, integer, rational and real. π is irrational and real.

2 + 3 = 5 rational. √4 + √9 = 2 + 3 = 5 rational. √2 + √3 irrational. 5 × 1/2 = 5/2 rational. 2 × √3 irrational. √8 ÷ √2 = √4 = 2 rational. π + 1 irrational. 0.5 + 0.333… = 5/6 rational. √25 – √16 = 5 – 4 = 1 rational. 3 × √5 irrational.
We write √2 ≈ 1.414, but √2 is not exactly 1.414; the decimal is a rational approximation. Likewise π ≈ 3.14 or 22/7. Note that 22/7 = 3.142857… is not equal to π.

Suppose √2 = p/q in lowest terms (p and q have no common factor). Then 2 = p²/q², so p² = 2q². So p² is even, so p is even; write p = 2k. Then 4k² = 2q², so q² = 2k², so q² is even and q is even. But then p and q are both even and share the factor 2, which contradicts 'lowest terms'. So √2 cannot be rational.

3 + 5 = 8 rational. √4 + √9 = 5 rational. √2 + √3 irrational. 5 × 1/2 = 5/2 rational. 2√3 irrational. √8 ÷ √2 = 2 rational. π + 1 irrational. 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 rational. √25 – √16 = 1 rational. 3√5 irrational.

title: Direct and Inverse Variation, with Powers
summary: The constant of variation, direct variation y = kx, inverse variation y = k/x, and variations with squares, cubes and square roots.

p: y varies directly as x means y = kx, where k is the constant of variation. We write y ∝ x. As x increases, y increases; y/x is constant; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
Example 1: y varies directly as x and y = 20 when x = 5. (a) k = 20 ÷ 5 = 4. (b) y = 4x. (c) when x = 8, y = 32.
Example 2: y = 12 when x = 3. Find y when x = 7. k = 4, so y = 28. Or use y₁/x₁ = y₂/x₂: 12/3 = y/7, so y = 28.
y varies inversely as x means y = k/x, so xy is constant. As x increases, y decreases.
Example 3: y = 6 when x = 4. k = 24, y = 24/x, so when x = 8, y = 3. Example 4: y = 10 when x = 5, so k = 50, y = 50/x; when y = 25, 25x = 50, so x = 2.
y ∝ x² means y = kx². Example 5: y = 18 when x = 3, so 18 = 9k, k = 2 and y = 2x². When x = 5, y = 50.
y ∝ √x means y = k√x. Example 6: y = 12 when x = 16, so 12 = 4k, k = 3. When x = 25, y = 3 × 5 = 15.
y ∝ x³ means y = kx³. Example 7: y = 24 when x = 2, so k = 3 and y = 3x³. When x = 3, y = 81.
y ∝ 1/x² means y = k/x². Example 8: y = 10 when x = 2, so k = 40 and y = 40/x². When x = 5, y = 40/25 = 1.6.
y ∝ 1/√x means y = k/√x. Example 9: y = 6 when x = 9, so k = 18 and y = 18/√x. When x = 4, y = 9.

sections.h: Steps to solve any variation problem
p: 1. Write the variation as an equation with k. 2. Put in the given pair of values and find k. 3. Write the full equation. 4. Put in the new value and find the answer.

title: Joint and Partial Variation
summary: Quantities that depend on two others multiplied together, and quantities with a fixed part plus a variable part, with business examples.

p: z varies jointly as x and y means z = kxy (z varies directly as the product of x and y).
Example 10: z = 24 when x = 2 and y = 3. k = 24 ÷ 6 = 4. When x = 4 and y = 5, z = 4 × 4 × 5 = 80.
Example 11: the area of a triangle varies jointly as the base and the height. A = 24 cm² when b = 6 and h = 8. k = 24 ÷ 48 = 1/2, which is the familiar A = ½bh. When b = 10 and h = 12, A = 60 cm².
Example 12: z varies jointly as x² and y; z = 108 when x = 3, y = 4. k = 108 ÷ (9 × 4) = 3. When x = 2 and y = 5: z = 3 × 4 × 5 = 60.
Partial variation has a part that varies and a part that is fixed: y = kx + c. You need two pairs of values to find k and c (two equations).
Example 13: y = 10 when x = 2 and y = 19 when x = 5. 10 = 2k + c and 19 = 5k + c. Subtract: 9 = 3k, so k = 3. Then 10 = 6 + c, so c = 4. The equation is y = 3x + 4, so when x = 8, y = 28.

Example 14: the cost C of making x items partly varies as x and is partly fixed. C = ₦500 at 10 items and ₦800 at 20 items. 500 = 10k + c and 800 = 20k + c. 300 = 10k, so k = 30 and c = 200. C = 30x + 200: fixed cost ₦200, cost per item ₦30, and for 50 items C = 1,500 + 200 = ₦1,700.
Example 15: y partly varies as x² and is partly constant: y = 7 at x = 1 and y = 16 at x = 2. 7 = k + c; 16 = 4k + c; so 9 = 3k, k = 3, c = 4. y = 3x² + 4, so at x = 3, y = 31.

title: Combined Variation and Real-Life Applications
summary: Variation that mixes direct and inverse parts, and uses in physics and business, with the answers to the remaining exercises.

p: Example 16: z varies directly as x and inversely as y, so z = kx/y. z = 15 when x = 6 and y = 2: 15 = 3k, k = 5. When x = 10 and y = 5: z = 5 × 10 ÷ 5 = 10.
Example 17: z varies directly as x² and inversely as √y: z = kx²/√y. z = 8 when x = 4 and y = 9: 8 = 16k/3, so k = 3/2. When x = 3, y = 4: z = (3/2) × 9 ÷ 2 = 27/4 = 6.75.
Example 18: z varies jointly as x and y and inversely as w: z = kxy/w. z = 6 when x = 2, y = 3, w = 4: 6 = 6k/4, so k = 4. When x = 5, y = 4, w = 2: z = 4 × 20 ÷ 2 = 40.
Hooke's law (physics): the extension of a spring varies directly as the force. 10 N gives 2 cm, so k = 0.2 and 25 N gives 5 cm.
Speed and time: time varies inversely as speed. 60 km/h takes 4 hours, so T = 240/S and at 80 km/h it takes 3 hours.
Cylinder: V varies jointly as the height and the square of the radius. V = 100π at r = 5, h = 4, so k = π and V = πr²h (the standard formula). For r = 3, h = 7: V = 63π.
Light (inverse square law): illumination varies inversely as the square of the distance. 100 lux at 2 m gives k = 400, so at 5 m the illumination is 400 ÷ 25 = 16 lux.

Electricity bill (partial variation): ₦2,500 for 100 units and ₦4,000 for 200 units. 100k = 1,500, so k = ₦15 per unit and the fixed charge is 2,500 – 1,500 = ₦1,000. For 350 units: 15 × 350 + 1,000 = ₦6,250.
